title: The Mountain's Accounts
synopsis: An unexplained tax record leads an archivist toward a hidden mountain town and a carefully concealed history.

records.text: The confederation's archive says the conquest ended centuries ago. Your grandmother says it never quite ended. While correcting old tax records, you find a mountain town that has paid its dues for eighty years but appears on no map.

choices.text: Trace the town through the archive's payment records
Ask your grandmother what the old khipu say

ledger.text: The payments change from maize to copper to electricity, always under the same name: Qhapaq Pampa. A clerk warns you that the town was classified after a dam was built there. The paper trail is real, but someone has been carefully deciding who may read it.

choices.text: Make copies before the archive can close the record
File a formal request and force the archive to answer

khipu.text: Your grandmother lays knotted cords across the table. Their pattern names a settlement beside a river and records a promise of shared water. She cannot prove it is Qhapaq Pampa, but she recognizes the name as one used by people who refused to disappear into an imperial census.

choices.text: Carry the cords with you as testimony
Leave the fragile cords safe and travel with only their story

text.value: In Qhapaq Pampa, elders recognize the name your grandmother spoke when you lay the khipu on the table. They show you a matching pattern in their own records. The cords are fragile, but now the town has seen them and can decide what to share. The dam lights their homes; a company keeps their promised share of its power.

In Qhapaq Pampa, elders recognize the name your grandmother spoke. You kept the khipu safe, so there is no document to place beside their records; instead, they correct your grandmother's story with details she could not have known. The dam lights their homes, but a company keeps their promised share of its power.

In Qhapaq Pampa, the old payment records match the town's own books. You brought copies before the archive could erase them; an elder asks you to leave one set with the people whose history it records. The dam lights their homes, but a company keeps their promised share of its power.

In Qhapaq Pampa, the archive finally answers your hearing request by confirming the payments, but the officials redact the people who made them. The town's own books fill in the missing names. The dam lights their homes, but a company keeps their promised share of its power.

choices.text: Publish the evidence and let the country argue in daylight
Help the town negotiate quietly for its share
Stay and help the community organize its own archive

public_hearing.text: The records become public. The company contests every page, and the town's elders choose which names may be printed. The confederation's water council opens a hearing that cannot be hidden. Qhapaq Pampa wins no instant electricity or apology; it wins the right to make its case where everyone can hear it, and the right to keep parts of its history private.

settlement.text: The company agrees to return part of the power revenue while the larger claim proceeds. Some villagers call it too little; others point to the school lights and clinic refrigerator. You helped secure an immediate, imperfect remedy instead of a public reckoning. The dispute remains, now written in a contract the town helped shape.

living_archive.text: Children record the elders' accounts beside the engineers' maps and, with the family's permission, the old khipu. The town is still contested, but no longer absent. Your grandmother says keeping a record is not the same as winning; it is how a people stays present for the next argument. You leave without settling who owns the story, and the children know that question belongs to them too.
